notes.title: Chapter map: OOP design

headings.text: 🌳 How should I add this behaviour?

notes.html:
The Python delta of object-oriented design: the principles live in the System Design LLD track, the mechanisms in sections 1, 4 and 8, and this chapter answers what changes when the language is Python. Read each arrow as a sentence: classmethod vs staticmethod built on descriptors.

Green = CORE, blue = SUPPORTING, grey = another chapter (dashed edges).

Reading order:88 encapsulation89 classmethod vs staticmethod90 __new__ vs __init__91 mixins92 composition & delegation94 patterns & SOLID, then drill with 95.

How should I add this behaviour?

The chapter's tools are alternatives for one question, so the tree lives here.

What each leaf is, and the one condition that would change the answer:

  • a function (patterns delta): if it later needs configuration that varies per use, bind it with functools.partial before reaching for a class.

  • a classmethod (89): if construction must return existing objects (interning, caching), that's __new__ instead.

  • 🎁 a wrapper (92): if callers use len(), [] or operators on it, you must define those dunders on the wrapper.

  • 🧷 a mixin (91): if the capability needs real state or differs per instance, it's a wrapper.

  • a subclass (LLD 08): if the subclass would refuse or weaken a parent method, it isn't an is-a; use a smaller Protocol.

  • 🦆 Protocol + composition (48): if implementations share real code, add an ABC base on top of the Protocol.

  • The one big idea: Python gives you functions, modules, descriptors and structural typing, so much of classic OOP ceremony (getters, factory classes, singletons, strategy hierarchies) becomes a plain feature. Design is choosing the least structure that keeps invariants and seams clear.

  • The two most-confused pairs: classmethod vs staticmethod (89: only one follows the subclass) · mixin vs wrapper (91 vs 92: onto a class at definition vs around an object at runtime).

  • Ten minutes before an interview: 89's binding sequence diagram, 92's wrapper stack, 94's pattern table, then this tree.

  • Cross-chapter: descriptors (property, classmethod) · MRO (super()) · LLD patterns (each pattern's intent).

notes.title: Encapsulation & the Public-API Boundary
notes.html:
References

Tutorial: private variables and name mangling · property · 📜 PEP 8: designing for inheritance

TL;DR

Python has no private: _x is a convention ("not public API"), and __x is name mangling that prevents subclass clashes, not access. Start with a plain attribute; when it needs logic, turn it into a @property without changing a single caller. That's why Python has no getter-first habit.

Flow:expose a plain attributelater a rule appears (validation, derived value)swap in @property with a setterevery obj.x and obj.x = … call site keeps workingmark internals _xuse __x only to stop a subclass from clobbering a name

Recall

Prompt Answer
What does _x mean? "Internal, not public API": a convention tools and readers respect; nothing enforces it.
What does __x actually do? Rewrites the name to _ClassName__x inside the class body, so a subclass's __x can't collide with it.
Can you still reach a __x attribute? Yes: obj._Account__pin. Mangling isn't access control.
Why no getters and setters by default? A property can replace an attribute later with the same obj.x syntax, so the upgrade path is free.
Property or method? Property for cheap, side-effect-free, attribute-like values; a method when it's costly, does I/O, or takes arguments.
Draw by hand: two pins Account.__pin → _Account__pin; Savings.__pin → _Savings__pin: both live in one instance __dict__.

The idea

In Java you write getBalance() on day one, because turning a public field into a method later breaks every caller. Python removed that reason. On CPython 3.12:

class Thermostat:                        # v1: a plain attribute
    def __init__(self, c): self.celsius = c

class Thermostat:                        # v2: a rule appeared, callers unchanged
    def __init__(self, c): self.celsius = c          # goes through the setter too
    @property
    def celsius(self): return self._c
    @celsius.setter
    def celsius(self, v):
        if v < -273.15: raise ValueError("below absolute zero")
        self._c = v

t = Thermostat(20); t.celsius = 25; t.celsius    # → 25, same syntax as v1
Thermostat(-300)                                   # → ValueError: below absolute zero

obj.celsius and obj.celsius = … work identically before and after, because property is a data descriptor that intercepts both. So in Python you expose plain attributes and promote them only when a rule appears. Encapsulation still matters, but its job is protecting invariants behind a small public surface (see LLD: encapsulation of invariants), not hiding fields behind ceremony.

The trade: Python trusts callers ("we're all consenting adults") and gives you a free upgrade path, and in exchange privacy is a convention you must signal clearly and keep.

How it works

Where the two pins actually live (dunder underscores escaped for the diagram):

Rule What actually happens
Mangling is compile-time Inside a class body, self.__pin is rewritten to self._Account__pin. The instance above held both _Account__pin and _Savings__pin side by side, and s.__pin from outside raised AttributeError: 'Savings' object has no attribute '__pin'.
Only leading double, no trailing __init__ and other dunders aren't mangled; __x__ is the language's namespace, never yours.
Properties cost a call Reading the property took ~24 ns against ~14 ns for a plain attribute (3.12, including a lambda's overhead): irrelevant except in hot loops.
Read-only by omission A property with no setter rejects assignment; __slots__ or a frozen dataclass stop new attributes.

Code

A public surface that's small, typed and invariant-safe:

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Wallet:
    owner: str                                  # public, plain: no rule needed
    _cents: int = field(default=0, repr=False)  # internal: the invariant lives here

    @property
    def balance(self) -> int:                   # read-only public view
        return self._cents

    def deposit(self, cents: int) -> None:      # a verb, not a setter: it has a rule
        if cents <= 0:
            raise ValueError("deposit must be positive")
        self._cents += cents

    def withdraw(self, cents: int) -> None:
        if cents > self._cents:
            raise ValueError("insufficient funds")
        self._cents -= cents

Three choices carry the design. owner stays a plain attribute because nothing constrains it. balance is a read-only property, so callers can't bypass the rules. And state changes are verbs (deposit, withdraw) rather than a balance setter, because "set the balance to X" isn't a domain operation. That's tell, don't ask in Python form.

Break it: treating __x as private.

class Account:
    def __init__(self): self.__pin = 1234
class Savings(Account):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.__pin = 9999          # a NEW attribute, not an override
s = Savings()
print(sorted(vars(s)), s._Account__pin)
# look for: two pins, and the parent's still readable from outside
# naive model predicts: Savings overrode a private pin, and nothing outside can read it

It printed ['_Account__pin', '_Savings__pin', '_balance'] 1234 on CPython 3.12. Mangling did its real job, keeping the subclass from silently clobbering the parent's name, and nothing else: anyone can read _Account__pin. Reach for __x in base classes designed for inheritance; use _x everywhere else.

Interview

30-second answer: Python has no enforced privacy. A single underscore marks something as internal by convention; a double underscore triggers name mangling to _Class__x, which exists to stop subclasses colliding with a base class's names, not to block access. Because @property can replace a plain attribute later with identical call syntax, you expose attributes directly and promote them when a rule appears. Encapsulation is about protecting invariants behind a small public surface, not getters.

Q · Mechanism — What exactly does name mangling do, and why does it exist? At compile time, inside a class body, any identifier __name without trailing underscores becomes _ClassName__name. So Account.__pin and Savings.__pin are two different attributes in the same instance dict, and a subclass can't accidentally overwrite its parent's internals. It's not access control: obj._Account__pin works, and so does getattr. Dunders like __init__ aren't mangled. Use it sparingly, mainly in base classes meant for subclassing by others.

Q · Failure — A teammate made every attribute __x "for safety", and now tests and subclasses break. What went wrong? Mangling binds names to the class that wrote them, so a subclass method that reads self.__x looks for _Subclass__x and misses the parent's value; mocks and tests patching obj.__x patch the wrong name; and debugging output is cluttered with _Class__x. The fix is _x for internal state, a small public API of methods and properties, and __x only where a base class must be robust against unknown subclasses.

Q · Design — Design the public API of a client class other teams will import, so you can evolve it for years. Expose the minimum: a few verbs and read-only properties, typed, with internals behind _. Plain attributes where nothing constrains them, knowing a property can replace them later. Declare the surface explicitly: __all__ at module level, a Protocol describing what callers may rely on (protocols), and a deprecation path (warnings.warn(..., DeprecationWarning)) before removing anything. It breaks when callers reach into _ names; make the public API complete enough that they don't need to.

Compare

x _x __x @property
Meaning public internal, by convention internal + mangled per class public, with logic behind it
Enforced? n/a no no (_C__x works) yes, for missing setters
Prevents nothing accidental use (by convention) subclass name clashes invalid writes, stale derived values
Use when no rule applies implementation details base classes for unknown subclasses a rule or computation appears

Pitfalls

  • "__x makes an attribute private"
    It mangles the name; obj._Class__x still reads it (see Break it).
  • "Good OOP means getters and setters for every field"
    In Python, start with attributes; a property upgrades them without breaking callers.
  • Not the same: property vs method
    ↳ Difference: a property promises cheap and side-effect-free; anything slow, I/O-bound or parameterised should be a method, so the call site looks like work.
  • Don't expose setters for state with rules.
    ↳ Why: balance = x bypasses the domain; use verbs (deposit, withdraw) that enforce invariants.
  • Don't let callers depend on _ names.
    ↳ Why: they'll break on your next refactor; if they need it, it belongs in the public API.
  • Don't put heavy work in a property getter.
    ↳ Why: obj.total in a loop looks free and isn't; cache it with cached_property or make it a method.

Connections

Path:descriptorsencapsulationclassmethod vs staticmethod
  • Builds on descriptors: property is a data descriptor, which is why it can replace an attribute.
  • Same idea elsewhere: LLD: encapsulation of invariants is the language-neutral principle this note applies.
  • Used by dataclasses: field(repr=False), frozen=True and init=False shape the public surface.
  • Contrasts with Java and C#: private fields plus getter-first, because a field can't become a method later without breaking callers.
  • Builds on protocols: a Protocol documents exactly which members callers may rely on.

notes.title: classmethod vs staticmethod — the Design Call
notes.html:
References

classmethod · staticmethod · Descriptor HowTo: functions and methods

TL;DR

A classmethod receives the class it was called on as cls, so cls(...) builds the right subclass: the tool for alternative constructors and factories. A staticmethod receives nothing; if it never needs the class and is never overridden, it usually belongs at module level.

Flow:DevConfig.from_dict(d)attribute lookup finds the classmethod in Configits descriptor binds cls = DevConfig (the caller, not the definer)cls(...) builds a DevConfiga staticmethod binds nothing, so a hard-coded Config(...) builds the parent

Recall

Prompt Answer
What does cls bind to? The class the method was called on (or the instance's class), not the class that defined it.
The canonical classmethod use? Alternative constructors: from_dict, from_env, from_config, which stay correct in subclasses.
When is a staticmethod a smell? Never called through the class, never overridden, doesn't need the class: make it a module function.
What does instance.from_env show? A bound method whose __self__ is the class; a staticmethod is a plain function.
How are they built? Both are descriptors: classmethod.__get__ binds the owner class; staticmethod.__get__ returns the raw function.
Draw by hand: who gets built DevConfig.from_dict ─▶ cls=DevConfig ─▶ DevConfig · DevConfig.make ─▶ Config(...) ─▶ Config

The idea

Python has one __init__, so "construct this from a dict, from the environment, from a file" can't be overloads. Classmethods are the answer, and the reason is what cls binds to. On CPython 3.12:

class Config:
    def __init__(self, host, port): self.host, self.port = host, port
    @classmethod
    def from_dict(cls, d): return cls(d["host"], d["port"])      # builds whatever cls is
    @staticmethod
    def make(d): return Config(d["host"], d["port"])            # hard-codes the parent

class DevConfig(Config): pass

type(DevConfig.from_dict(d)).__name__   # → 'DevConfig'
type(DevConfig.make(d)).__name__        # → 'Config': the subclass silently lost

The staticmethod version works until someone subclasses, then returns the wrong type with no error. That's the whole design call: if the method creates or describes the class, it's a classmethod; if it's a helper that merely lives nearby, it's a staticmethod, or better, a plain function in the module.

The trade: classmethods give subclass-correct construction and per-class behaviour for one extra parameter, and staticmethods give namespacing only, which a module already provides.

How it works

How each decorator binds, through the descriptor protocol:

Rule What actually happens
Classmethod binding classmethod.__get__(obj, owner) returns a method bound to owner; on 3.12, OpenAIClient("x").from_env printed <bound method LLMClient.from_env of <class 'OpenAIClient'>>.
Staticmethod binding staticmethod.__get__ returns the underlying function untouched: <function LLMClient.estimate_tokens ...>.
Overriding Both can be overridden in a subclass; only a classmethod can call other overridden classmethods through cls.
Inside the class dict type(LLMClient.__dict__["from_env"]) is classmethod; the decorator objects are what sit in the dict, not functions.

Code

A provider factory that stays subclass-correct, with a registry filled by __init_subclass__:

import os

class LLMClient:
    _registry: dict[str, type["LLMClient"]] = {}

    def __init_subclass__(cls, provider: str = "", **kw):      # runs when a subclass is defined
        super().__init_subclass__(**kw)
        if provider:
            LLMClient._registry[provider] = cls

    def __init__(self, model: str, timeout_s: float = 30.0):
        self.model, self.timeout_s = model, timeout_s

    @classmethod
    def from_config(cls, cfg: dict) -> "LLMClient":           # a factory: picks the subclass
        return cls._registry[cfg["provider"]](cfg["model"], cfg.get("timeout_s", 30.0))

    @classmethod
    def from_env(cls) -> "LLMClient":                         # alternative constructor
        return cls(os.environ.get("LLM_MODEL", "small"))

    @staticmethod
    def estimate_tokens(text: str) -> int:                    # needs nothing from the class
        return max(1, len(text) // 4)

class OpenAIClient(LLMClient, provider="openai"): pass
class AnthropicClient(LLMClient, provider="anthropic"): pass

On 3.12, LLMClient.from_config({"provider": "anthropic", "model": "m"}) returned an AnthropicClient, OpenAIClient.from_env() an OpenAIClient, and the registry held ['anthropic', 'openai'] without any import-time wiring. estimate_tokens is the honest staticmethod: tied to the domain, needs no class. If nothing ever overrides it, a module-level estimate_tokens() is simpler still.

Break it: the staticmethod factory.

class Config:
    def __init__(self, host, port): self.host, self.port = host, port
    @staticmethod
    def from_dict(d): return Config(d["host"], d["port"])
class DevConfig(Config):
    def debug_url(self): return f"http://{self.host}:{self.port}/debug"
cfg = DevConfig.from_dict({"host": "localhost", "port": 8000})
cfg.debug_url()
# look for: the type of cfg
# naive model predicts: a DevConfig, because we called it on DevConfig

cfg is a plain Config, so debug_url() raises AttributeError, far from the cause. The factory hard-coded its class. A classmethod with cls(...) fixes it in one line, and every future subclass inherits the fix.

Interview

30-second answer: A classmethod receives the class it was called on as cls, so it's the tool for alternative constructors like from_dict or from_env and for factories: cls(...) builds the correct subclass automatically. A staticmethod receives nothing; it's a function that lives in the class namespace. If it doesn't need the class and is never overridden, it's usually clearer as a module-level function. Both are implemented as descriptors.

Q · Mechanism — How does Python decide what cls is? Attribute lookup finds the classmethod object in the class __dict__ (or an ancestor's) and calls its __get__(instance, owner). It returns a method bound to owner, the class the lookup started from, or type(instance) when called on an instance. So the binding follows the caller, not the definer. staticmethod.__get__ returns the raw function, binding nothing, which is why it can't know which subclass invoked it.

Q · Failure — A subclass's factory returns parent instances, and a method missing on them fails in production. Diagnose. The factory is a staticmethod (or a classmethod that calls the parent by name instead of cls), so construction ignores which class it was called on (see Break it). Fix: classmethod plus cls(...); add a test that each subclass's from_* returns that subclass. Watch for the same bug in copy/__reduce__ implementations and __add__ that return ParentClass(...) instead of type(self)(...).

Q · Design — Design construction for a family of provider clients configured from YAML, env vars and tests. One __init__ taking explicit, typed parameters, and classmethods for each source (from_config, from_env), each normalising input then calling cls(...). Subclasses register themselves with __init_subclass__(provider=…), so adding a provider is one class and no edit to a central if/elif (open-closed, Python's way). Tests construct directly with __init__. It breaks if a subclass changes the __init__ signature; keep it stable or override the classmethods too.

Compare

instance method classmethod staticmethod module function
First argument the instance the class it was called on none none
Subclass-aware via type(self) via cls
Overridable
Use for behaviour on state constructors, factories, class-level config a helper tied to the class's concept everything else

Pitfalls

  • "A staticmethod is just a classmethod without cls"
    Losing cls loses subclass correctness (see Break it).
  • "Utility functions belong in a class as staticmethods"
    Python has modules; a staticmethod nobody overrides is a module function in a costume.
  • Not the same as Java's static
    ↳ Difference: Java's static factory can't be polymorphic; Python's classmethod is, because cls follows the caller.
  • Don't name the class inside its own classmethod.
    ↳ Why: return Config(...) reintroduces the staticmethod bug; write cls(...).
  • Don't let subclasses change __init__'s signature casually.
    ↳ Why: inherited from_* constructors call cls(...) with the parent's arguments.
  • 🔖 Version: chaining @classmethod over @property was deprecated in 3.11 and removed in 3.13; use a metaclass property or a plain classmethod.
    ↳ Note: examples run on CPython 3.12.13.

Connections

Path:descriptorsclassmethod vs staticmethod__new__ vs __init__
  • Builds on descriptors: both decorators are descriptors with different __get__.
  • Builds on __init_subclass__: the registry that makes the factory open for extension.
  • Used by patterns, the Python delta: Factory in Python is a classmethod or a registry.
  • Same idea elsewhere: LLD: factory and abstract factory is the language-neutral pattern this implements.
  • Contrasts with Java's static factories: not polymorphic, so Java needs a separate factory class where Python needs one decorator.

notes.title: __new__ vs __init__ — When Construction Is the Problem
notes.html:
References

Data model: object.__new__ · Data model: object.__init__

TL;DR

__new__(cls, …) creates and returns the object; __init__(self, …) fills in the one it's given and returns None. You need __new__ only when creation itself must change: subclassing an immutable, or returning a cached instance.

Flow:C(args)type.__call__C.__new__(C, args) returns an objectis it an instance of C? yes: obj.__init__(args) runs; no: __init__ is skippedthe object is returned to the caller

Recall

Prompt Answer
Why can't __init__ customise a tuple or float subclass? The value is fixed when __new__ creates the object; by __init__ it's too late.
When does __init__ not run? When __new__ returns something that isn't an instance of cls.
Why is the __new__ singleton a trap? __init__ re-runs on every call, so state is silently reset; it also hides a global.

The idea

Construction is two steps, and almost all classes only need the second. On CPython 3.12:

class Celsius(float):
    def __new__(cls, v):
        if v < -273.15: raise ValueError("below absolute zero")
        return super().__new__(cls, v)          # the value is set HERE
Celsius(21.5) + 1                                # → 22.5, a real float

class Point(tuple):
    def __init__(self, x, y): pass              # too late: tuple.__new__ already ran
Point(1, 2)   # → TypeError: tuple expected at most 1 argument, got 2

An immutable's value is decided when __new__ builds it, so validation and conversion for int, float, str and tuple subclasses belong there. The other legitimate use is returning an existing object: interning, caching, flyweights. Everything else, including "configure the new object", is __init__'s job.

The trade: __new__ gives control over which object exists, and in exchange it runs before any state, interacts with __init__ in surprising ways, and is rarely the clearest tool.

How it works

Rule What actually happens
__new__ is implicitly static It takes cls explicitly and must return the object; super().__new__(cls) allocates one.
The skip rule A __new__ returning an unrelated Other() gave back an Other, and C.__init__ never ran.
A cached object still gets __init__ Returning a cached instance of cls re-runs __init__ on it every call: the singleton trap.
Metaclass level type.__call__ drives both steps, which is why a metaclass can intercept construction (metaclasses).

Code

Interning value objects: equal codes share one instance, and no __init__ exists to re-run:

import weakref

class Currency:
    _cache: "weakref.WeakValueDictionary[str, Currency]" = weakref.WeakValueDictionary()
    __slots__ = ("code", "__weakref__")

    def __new__(cls, code: str):
        code = code.upper()
        obj = cls._cache.get(code)
        if obj is None:                    # create once per code
            obj = super().__new__(cls)
            obj.code = code                # all setup here: there is no __init__
            cls._cache[code] = obj
        return obj

On 3.12, Currency("inr") is Currency("INR") was True. The WeakValueDictionary lets unused currencies be collected (weakrefs), so the cache can't leak. Putting the setup in __new__ and having no __init__ is the point: there's nothing to re-run.

Break it: the __new__ singleton.

class Singleton:
    _inst = None
    def __new__(cls, *a, **k):
        if cls._inst is None:
            cls._inst = super().__new__(cls)
        return cls._inst
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
x = Singleton("db"); y = Singleton("cache")
print(x is y, x.name)
# look for: what x.name is now
# naive model predicts: True db — one instance, created once

It printed True cache: same object, but __init__ ran twice and overwrote the first caller's state. It's also not thread-safe (two threads can both see _inst is None) and it hides a global behind constructor syntax. In Python the singleton answer is a module-level instance, or an instance created once and injected (patterns, the Python delta).

Interview

30-second answer: __new__ creates the object: it receives the class and returns an instance. __init__ initialises the instance it's given and returns None. You need __new__ only when creation itself must change: subclassing immutables like str, int or tuple, whose value is fixed at creation, or returning cached instances. __init__ runs only if __new__ returns an instance of the class.

Q · Mechanism — What happens, step by step, when you call C(args)? type.__call__(C, args) calls C.__new__(C, args), which allocates or fetches an object. If the result is an instance of C, it then calls obj.__init__(args) and returns the object; otherwise it returns whatever __new__ produced without calling __init__. That's why a caching __new__ that returns an existing instance still triggers __init__ (resetting state), and why returning a different type skips it.

Compare

__new__ __init__
Receives cls self, already created
Returns the object (required) None (anything else is a TypeError)
Use for immutable subclasses, caching, interning ordinary setup and validation
Runs always only if __new__ returned an instance of cls

Pitfalls

  • "__init__ is the constructor"
    __new__ constructs; __init__ initialises, which only matters when creation itself must change.
  • "A __new__ singleton gives one, initialised-once instance"
    One instance, initialised on every call (see Break it).
  • Not the same as a factory classmethod
    ↳ Difference: a classmethod factory is explicit and named (from_dict); __new__ changes what plain C(...) returns, which surprises readers.
  • Don't override __new__ for ordinary validation.
    ↳ Instead: __init__, __post_init__ on a dataclass, or a classmethod.
  • Don't cache in __new__ while also defining __init__.
    ↳ Why: every lookup re-initialises the cached object.

Connections

Path:classmethod vs staticmethod__new__ vs __init__mixins
  • Builds on dunder protocols: construction is two dunders called by type.__call__.
  • Builds on metaclasses: a metaclass's __call__ can intercept both steps.
  • Contrasts with classmethod factories: explicit alternative construction instead of a changed C(...).
  • Same idea elsewhere: LLD: singleton done correctly reaches the same verdict in Java terms.

notes.title: Multiple Inheritance & Mixin Design
notes.html:
References

Tutorial: multiple inheritance · Raymond Hettinger: Python's super() considered super!

TL;DR

A mixin adds one narrow capability, holds little or no state, sits before the concrete base, and calls super() so the chain continues. Cooperative super() runs each __init__ exactly once along the MRO; calling Parent.__init__(self) by name runs a shared base twice.

Flow:class Client(LoggingMixin, CacheMixin, Base)C3 builds the MRO: Client, Logging, Cache, Base, objecteach __init__ takes its own keyword, then super().__init__(**kw)super() means next in the instance's MRO, not "my parent"every class runs once

Recall

Prompt Answer
The mixin rules? One responsibility, little or no state, **kw passed through super(), listed before the base, named *Mixin.
What does super() call? The next class in type(self).__mro__ after the current one, which may be a sibling, not the parent.
Why does Parent.__init__(self) break a diamond? Each branch calls the shared base directly, so it runs twice; add a third base and the order is wrong too.

The idea

Multiple inheritance in Python is safe when every class cooperates, and broken when any one doesn't. Same diamond twice, on CPython 3.12:

__init__ style Order of __init__ calls
each calls super().__init__(**kw) Client, Logging, Cache, Base
each calls its parent by name Client, Logging, Base, Cache, Base

With names hard-coded, Base.__init__ ran twice (resetting whatever it set up the first time), because LoggingMixin didn't know CacheMixin would come next. With super(), each class hands off to the next class in this instance's MRO, so the chain visits everyone exactly once whatever the combination. That's why mixins must call super() even when their own parent looks like object.

The trade: mixins let you compose small behaviours onto a class without wrappers, and in exchange every class in the hierarchy must cooperate, and the MRO becomes part of your design.

How it works

The client from the Code section, and the order super() follows:

OpenAIClient.__mro__ was OpenAIClient, JsonMixin, TimingMixin, BaseClient, object: left-to-right bases, each before anything it inherits from (C3 linearisation). TimingMixin.call wraps the call and passes it on with super().call(...), which reaches BaseClient.call only because TimingMixin is listed before it.

Code

import json, logging, time

class JsonMixin:
    """Adds to_json(). No state of its own, so it needs no __init__."""
    def to_json(self) -> str:
        return json.dumps({k: v for k, v in vars(self).items() if not k.startswith("_")})

class TimingMixin:
    """Logs slow calls. Takes its own keyword, passes the rest on."""
    def __init__(self, *, slow_ms: float = 500, **kw):
        self._slow_ms = slow_ms
        super().__init__(**kw)                     # next in the MRO, whoever that is
    def call(self, prompt: str) -> str:
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        try:
            return super().call(prompt)
        finally:
            if (ms := (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000) > self._slow_ms:
                logging.getLogger(type(self).__name__).warning("slow call %.0f ms", ms)

class BaseClient:
    def __init__(self, *, model: str, **kw):
        self.model = model
        super().__init__(**kw)                     # ends at object.__init__()
    def call(self, prompt: str) -> str:
        return f"{self.model}: {prompt}"

class OpenAIClient(JsonMixin, TimingMixin, BaseClient):   # mixins first, base last
    pass

OpenAIClient(model="gpt-x", slow_ms=10).call("hi") logged slow call 23 ms (with a 20 ms simulated call) and returned gpt-x: hi; to_json() gave {"model": "gpt-x"}. Keyword-only arguments make the chain safe: each class takes its own and forwards the rest. A typo surfaces at the end of the chain: retries=3 reached object.__init__ and raised TypeError: object.__init__() takes exactly one argument.

Interview

30-second answer: A mixin is a small class that adds one capability, like logging, serialisation or timing, to classes that inherit from it. Rules: one responsibility, little or no state, list it before the concrete base, and always call super() with **kwargs passed through. That cooperation is what makes a diamond work: super() follows the instance's MRO, so every __init__ runs exactly once.

Q · Mechanism — Why does super() sometimes call a sibling rather than the parent? super() inside class X means "the class after X in type(self).__mro__". The MRO is computed per final class by C3 linearisation, so for Client(LoggingMixin, CacheMixin, Base) the class after LoggingMixin is CacheMixin, a sibling that LoggingMixin never named. That's the feature: a mixin can wrap behaviour without knowing what it's combined with. It's also why one class calling its parent by name breaks the chain for everyone after it.

Compare

Mixin Composition (wrapper) ABC / Protocol
Adds behaviour onto a class behaviour around an object a contract, little or no behaviour
Combined at class definition runtime, by wiring class definition or by shape
Order matters yes: MRO yes: wrapping order no
Best for small, reusable capabilities (to_json, logging) swappable, stackable behaviour (retry, cache) interfaces

Pitfalls

  • "super() calls my parent"
    It calls the next class in the instance's MRO, which may be a sibling.
  • "Calling Parent.__init__(self) is more explicit, so safer"
    It runs a shared base twice in a diamond (see The idea).
  • Not the same as composition
    ↳ Difference: a mixin is fixed at class definition; a wrapper is chosen at runtime and can be swapped or stacked differently per instance.
  • Don't give mixins significant state or required positional arguments.
    ↳ Why: positional arguments can't be routed through an unknown chain; use keyword-only arguments.
  • Don't list a mixin after the concrete base.
    ↳ Why: the base's method is found first, so the mixin's override never runs.

Connections

Path:MROmixinscomposition & delegation
  • Builds on attribute lookup and the MRO: C3 decides who super() calls.
  • Contrasts with composition & delegation: behaviour around an object instead of onto a class.
  • Same idea elsewhere: LLD: composition over inheritance gives the general rule for when inheritance stops being worth it.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Django's class-based views and DRF build views from mixins, the canonical real-world example; Scala traits and Ruby modules are linearised the same way.

notes.title: Composition & Delegation in Python
notes.html:
References

Data model: __getattr__ · Data model: special method lookup · typing.Protocol

TL;DR

The principle ("has-a over is-a") lives in the LLD notes; Python's delta is how you compose: small wrappers typed by a Protocol, stacked at runtime. __getattr__ forwards ordinary attributes for free, but implicit dunder lookups go to the type and bypass it: a proxy gets no len(), [] or in.

Flow:define the seam as a Protocoleach concern (retry, cache, metrics) is a wrapper holding an inner object of that typeit overrides only the methods it changes__getattr__ forwards everything elsewrappers stack in any order: N concerns stay N classes, not N×M subclasses

Recall

Prompt Answer
The class-explosion smell? CachedRetryingOpenAIClient: one subclass per combination, N×M classes instead of N + M.
What does __getattr__ forward? Ordinary lookups that fail normally (proxy.model, proxy.count).
Why does len(proxy) fail? Implicit special-method lookup goes to type(proxy), never the instance, so __getattr__ isn't consulted; define dunders explicitly.

The idea

The design argument for composition is in LLD 08: inheritance couples you to a base class's internals and multiplies classes per combination. Python makes the composed version unusually cheap, because the seam is a Protocol (no shared base needed) and forwarding is one method. With a fake provider that times out once, on CPython 3.12:

client: ChatModel = Cached(Retrying(FakeOpenAI()))
client.complete("hi")      # → answer to 'hi'   (1st upstream call timed out, retry succeeded)
client.complete("hi")      # → answer to 'hi'   (served from the cache)
client.model               # → 'gpt-x'          (forwarded through two __getattr__s)
# upstream calls: 2

Swapping the order, adding metrics, or using a different provider is wiring, not a new class. The catch is Python-specific: __getattr__ only runs for normal lookups. A proxy around a list answered p.count(2) → 1, but len(p) raised TypeError: object of type 'Proxy' has no len(), p[0] said 'Proxy' object is not subscriptable, and 2 in p said argument of type 'Proxy' is not iterable.

The trade: wrappers keep each concern in one small class and combine freely at runtime, and in exchange forwarding is explicit work, and dunders never forward on their own.

How it works

What each wrapper owns, and how a call travels down the stack:

Rule What actually happens
__getattr__ is a fallback It runs only after normal lookup (instance dict, class, MRO) fails, so methods a wrapper defines win.
Dunders skip the instance len(x), x[i], x + y look up type(x).__len__ etc. directly (attribute lookup), so a proxy must define each dunder it supports. A ListProxy with __len__ and __getitem__ then gave len 3, [0] 1, and in worked through the __getitem__ fallback.
Typing still holds mypy --strict (2.4.0) accepted client: ChatModel = Cached(Retrying(raw)): __getattr__ returning Any satisfies the Protocol's model.

Code

from typing import Any, Protocol

class ChatModel(Protocol):                       # the seam: anything with this shape fits
    model: str
    def complete(self, prompt: str) -> str: ...

class Cached:
    def __init__(self, inner: ChatModel) -> None:
        self._inner = inner
        self._cache: dict[str, str] = {}
    def complete(self, prompt: str) -> str:      # the one method this concern changes
        if prompt not in self._cache:
            self._cache[prompt] = self._inner.complete(prompt)
        return self._cache[prompt]
    def __getattr__(self, name: str) -> Any:     # everything else: forward
        return getattr(self._inner, name)

class Retrying:
    def __init__(self, inner: ChatModel, attempts: int = 3) -> None:
        self._inner, self._attempts = inner, attempts
    def complete(self, prompt: str) -> str:
        for attempt in range(1, self._attempts + 1):
            try:
                return self._inner.complete(prompt)
            except TimeoutError:
                if attempt == self._attempts:
                    raise
        raise AssertionError("unreachable")
    def __getattr__(self, name: str) -> Any:
        return getattr(self._inner, name)

client: ChatModel = Cached(Retrying(make_provider(cfg)))   # wiring, not subclassing

Each wrapper is testable alone with a fake inner object, and order is a decision you can see: Cached(Retrying(...)) retries only on cache misses, while Retrying(Cached(...)) would also retry cache lookups. Production retry logic belongs in reliability mechanics (backoff, classification); this shows only the shape.

Interview

30-second answer: Composition means building behaviour by holding collaborators rather than inheriting from them. In Python the seam is a Protocol, so any object with the right shape fits, and each concern (retry, caching, metrics) is a small wrapper that overrides one method and forwards the rest with __getattr__. That turns N×M subclasses into N wrappers stacked at runtime. The trap: implicit dunder calls like len() or [] bypass __getattr__, so a proxy must define them.

Q · Mechanism — Why doesn't __getattr__ make len(proxy) work? Implicit special-method invocation looks the method up on the type, not the instance, partly for speed and partly so that, for example, calling hash on a class uses the metaclass's method rather than the class's own. __getattr__ is only consulted when normal attribute lookup on the instance fails, and implicit lookup never goes through the instance. So proxy.__len__() works (explicit lookup, forwarded), but len(proxy) raises TypeError. The fix is defining each needed dunder on the proxy class.

Compare

Subclass per combination Wrapper stack Mixins
Classes for N concerns × M providers N × M N + M N + M, fixed per class
Combined at definition at runtime, per instance at definition
Order visible hidden in the hierarchy in the wiring line in the MRO (mixins)
Dunders inherited must be defined on the wrapper inherited

Pitfalls

  • "__getattr__ makes a perfect transparent proxy"
    Implicit dunder lookups bypass it: len, [], in, +, == all need explicit methods.
  • "Composition needs a common abstract base class"
    A Protocol is enough; vendor clients and fakes fit without inheriting anything.
  • Not the same as the @decorator syntax
    ↳ Difference: a wrapper object is the Decorator pattern (wrapping an object); @decorator wraps a function at definition (decorators).
  • Don't let __getattr__ recurse before _inner exists.
    ↳ Why: copy.copy and unpickling build objects without __init__, so self._inner calls __getattr__("_inner") again: copy.copy(proxy)._inner raised RecursionError on 3.12. Guard: if name == "_inner": raise AttributeError(name).
  • Don't monkey-patch where you could wrap.
    ↳ Why: a patch is global and invisible; a wrapper is local and in the wiring (monkey patching).

Connections

Path:mixinscomposition & delegationpatterns, the Python delta
  • Same idea elsewhere: LLD 08: composition over inheritance is the principle; this note is the Python mechanics.
  • Builds on attribute lookup: why __getattr__ is a fallback and dunders skip the instance.
  • Builds on protocols: the seam each wrapper accepts and satisfies.
  • Used by patterns, the Python delta: Decorator, Adapter and Proxy are all this wrapper shape.
  • Contrasts with mixins: behaviour onto a class, fixed at definition, instead of around an object.

notes.title: Patterns & SOLID — the Python Delta
notes.html:
References

Peter Norvig: design patterns in dynamic languages · Brandon Rhodes: Python design patterns · typing.Protocol

TL;DR

Many GoF patterns exist to work around a language without first-class functions, modules or generators; in Python several of them collapse into a feature. The senior signal is naming which patterns you deleted, and keeping the ones that still model something: Adapter, Decorator (object), Observer, State, Template Method.

Flow:read the pattern's intent (the LLD note)ask "does Python already give me this?"function, module, generator, partial, classmethod: use it and delete the classstill need polymorphic objects with state? keep the pattern, typed by a ProtocolSOLID's seams become small Protocols and injected callables

Recall

Prompt Answer
Which patterns does Python delete? Strategy and Command → functions (partial for bound arguments); Singleton → a module; Iterator → generators; Factory → classmethod or a dict registry.
Which still earn their keep? Adapter (vendor clients), Decorator as object wrapping, Observer, State, Template Method, Repository.
ISP and DIP in Python? ISP → small Protocols; DIP → inject callables or Protocols, which is really a testability argument.
OCP in Python? A registry filled by __init_subclass__ or a dict: new behaviour is a new class or function, not an edited if/elif.
What LSP violation can a type checker catch? Signature changes (mypy: Signature of "save" incompatible with supertype); not behavioural ones like raising where the parent didn't.
Draw by hand: Strategy, both ways Java: Ranker interface ◁─ three classes, injected into Search. Python: Callable[[docs], docs] + three functions in a dict.

The idea

Peter Norvig's 1996 talk showed 16 of the 23 GoF patterns becoming invisible or simpler in dynamic languages (Lisp and Dylan); Python inherits most of that. The intent of each pattern still matters, and the LLD notes teach it; what changes is the amount of structure needed to express it. Strategy on CPython 3.12:

def by_recency(docs): return sorted(docs, key=lambda d: d["ts"], reverse=True)
def by_score(docs):   return sorted(docs, key=lambda d: d["score"], reverse=True)
RANKERS = {"recency": by_recency, "score": by_score}     # the whole "pattern"

RANKERS["score"](docs)     # ids → [1, 2]
RANKERS["recency"](docs)   # ids → [2, 1]

No RankingStrategy interface, no concrete strategy classes, no context class: a function is an object with one method. The same move deletes Command (functools.partial(send, "email") in a queue), Iterator (a generator), Singleton (a module, which the import system already caches as one instance) and most Factories (a classmethod or registry). What survives is anything that needs state plus polymorphism: an Adapter around a vendor SDK, a State machine, an Observer list, wrapper objects.

The trade: Python lets you express a pattern's intent with far less structure, and in exchange the pattern's name is no longer visible in the code, so you name it in a docstring or a type alias.

How it works

The same Strategy, Java-shaped and Python-shaped:

The pattern catalogue, through Python's lens:

Pattern (LLD) In Python Keep a class?
Strategy · Command a function; partial for bound arguments; a dict for selection unless it carries state
Singleton a module-level instance, created once and injected (the __new__ version is a trap)
Factory classmethod + cls(...), or a registry via __init_subclass__ no separate factory class
Iterator a generator function
Decorator (object) · Proxy · Adapter a wrapper holding a Protocol-typed inner object (composition)
Observer · State · Template Method · Repository callables in a list; a class per state; an ABC with abstract hooks; a class per aggregate

Code

SOLID's Python form, in one provider seam:

from collections.abc import Callable
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from typing import Protocol

class Completer(Protocol):                       # ISP: the smallest interface callers need
    def complete(self, prompt: str) -> str: ...

class Embedder(Protocol):                        # a separate seam, not one fat "LLMClient"
    def embed(self, text: str) -> list[float]: ...

Clock = Callable[[], datetime]                   # DIP: depend on a callable, not datetime.now

class AnswerService:                             # SRP: answers questions, nothing else
    def __init__(self, llm: Completer, clock: Clock = lambda: datetime.now(timezone.utc)):
        self._llm, self._clock = llm, clock      # injected: fakes need no patching
    def answer(self, q: str) -> dict[str, str]:
        return {"text": self._llm.complete(q), "at": self._clock().isoformat()}

class Provider:                                  # OCP: a new provider is a new class
    registry: dict[str, type["Provider"]] = {}
    def __init_subclass__(cls, name: str = "", **kw: object) -> None:
        super().__init_subclass__(**kw)
        if name:
            Provider.registry[name] = cls

A test passes a FakeCompleter and clock=lambda: frozen_time; no mock.patch and no inheritance, because both seams are structural (protocols). Injecting a clock made a five-minute token report expired: True after advancing a fake clock six minutes, with no sleeping. That's the real argument for DIP in Python: testability, not abstraction for its own sake (LLD: constructor DI).

Break it: an LSP violation the type checker can't see.

class Store:
    def save(self, key: str, val: bytes) -> None: ...
class ReadOnlyStore(Store):
    def save(self, key: str, val: bytes) -> None:
        raise PermissionError("read-only")       # same signature, broken promise
def backup(s: Store) -> str:
    s.save("k", b"v"); return "ok"
backup(ReadOnlyStore())
# look for: does mypy warn?
# naive model predicts: the type checker enforces substitutability

mypy 2.4.0 reported nothing, and at runtime backup raised PermissionError: read-only. Change the signature instead (def save(self, key: str)) and mypy does catch it: Signature of "save" incompatible with supertype "Store". Types enforce the shape of LSP; only contract tests run against every subclass enforce the behaviour. The fix here is a design one: a read-only store isn't a Store; give readers a smaller Reader protocol.

Interview

30-second answer: Many GoF patterns compensate for languages without first-class functions or modules, so in Python several collapse: Strategy and Command become functions, Singleton is a module, Iterator is a generator, Factory is a classmethod or registry. The ones that model state plus polymorphism still earn their keep: Adapter, wrapping Decorators, Observer, State, Template Method. SOLID translates too: small Protocols for interface segregation, injected callables for dependency inversion, registries for open-closed.

Q · Mechanism — Why is a module a better singleton than a __new__-based class? The import system executes a module once per process and caches it in sys.modules, so every importer gets the same object, under the import lock, with no extra code. A __new__ singleton re-runs __init__ on every call, isn't thread-safe without a lock, and disguises global state as construction. Better still: create the one instance at startup and inject it, so tests can replace it; the module-level instance is the fallback, not the goal (LLD: singleton done correctly).

Q · Failure — A codebase has AbstractRankingStrategyFactory and twelve one-method classes. What do you do? That's Java-shaped Python: every one-method class with no state is a function, and a factory that only picks one is a dict lookup. Refactor in steps: type the seam as Callable[[list[Doc]], list[Doc]], convert the classes to functions, replace the factory with a registry dict, and keep a class only where state or several related methods appear. Tests usually shrink with it. Watch that public import paths keep working, or add deprecation aliases (LLD: pattern overuse).

Q · Design — Design the provider layer of an AI service so new providers, retries and caching never require editing existing code. A small Completer Protocol as the seam; an Adapter class per vendor SDK registered through __init_subclass__(name=…); a classmethod from_config choosing one by name; cross-cutting behaviour as wrapper objects stacked in one wiring function (composition); the service receives a Completer by injection. That's open-closed (new provider = new class), interface segregation (completion separate from embedding) and dependency inversion (the service never imports a vendor). It breaks when adapters leak vendor-specific errors; translate them at the adapter (custom exceptions).

Compare

SOLID principle (LLD 06) Java-shaped answer Python-shaped answer
Single responsibility one class, one reason to change the same, at module level too
Open-closed abstract base + subclasses + factory registry via __init_subclass__ or a dict
Liskov substitution enforced by inheritance + types signatures checked by mypy; behaviour by contract tests
Interface segregation many small interfaces many small Protocols, satisfied without inheriting
Dependency inversion DI container, interfaces constructor arguments typed by Protocols or Callable

Pitfalls

  • "Using patterns makes code more professional"
    A pattern Python already provides is ceremony; name the patterns you deleted.
  • "SOLID needs abstract base classes everywhere"
    Protocols and callables give the same seams with no inheritance tree.
  • Not the same: Decorator pattern vs @decorator
    ↳ Difference: the pattern wraps an object at runtime; @decorator wraps a function at definition (decorators).
  • Don't make a one-method stateless class.
    ↳ Why: it's a function in a costume; Strategy, Command and Handler classes are the usual offenders.
  • Don't trust the type checker for LSP.
    ↳ Why: it checks signatures, not promises (see Break it); run contract tests against every implementation.
  • Don't import a vendor SDK in domain code.
    ↳ Why: that's the dependency DIP inverts; inject an adapter typed by a Protocol.

Connections

Path:composition & delegationpatterns & SOLID, the Python deltaLLD design patterns
  • Same idea elsewhere: the LLD pattern catalogue teaches each pattern's intent; this note says what's left of it in Python.
  • Builds on first-class functions: why Strategy and Command collapse.
  • Builds on generators: why Iterator collapses.
  • Builds on protocols: the seams ISP and DIP need, without inheritance.
  • Builds on __init_subclass__: open-closed registries.
